correctness.rationale: For odd p, the p^j summand in the valuation of a(n,k) counts multiples in [n-k+1,n+k] minus floor(k/p^j). It is nonnegative. For k>=2, every p^j hitting the four central integers contributes at least one: for p^j>k this is direct, and for p^j<=k use floor(2k/p^j)-floor(k/p^j)>=1. Only 3 can hit two of the four integers at the same power, precisely at power 3 and n=1 mod 3. Degree two attains every predicted odd-prime minimum except this case. Then degree four exists, its four added factors are all units mod 3, and its factorial denominator removes one factor of 3. For k equal to the largest power of two <=n, k is even, and 2k+(n-k) has no binary carries, so binom(n+k,2k)(2k-1)!! is odd. This settles the gcd for all n>=2, including n=2,3 with only one retained coefficient.
residual_risks: The finite replay checks coefficients and contents in its stated range only; the all-index result follows from the valuation proof.

value.rationale: The even projection is the natural parity component (after removing the unit constant); its primitive integer normalization and prime reductions require its exact content, not just an obvious divisor of the Bessel row. The all-index classification identifies a single exceptional odd-prime loss and supplies an even-degree odd witness in every order. This is a modest but complete arithmetic invariant of a standard family, not a proposed new general theory.
residual_risks: No broader generalized Bessel classification or downstream application is established.
